title: Will it become harder to oversee AI systems?
date_source: Blog page byline dates the post 'May 21, 2026'; the linked full report (Loss of Oversight: How AI Systems May Become Harder to Audit, Monitor, and Investigate, UK AISI) carries no separate dated release, so the blog date is used.
rule_cited: §1 in scope (government AISI, sole author); §2 documented process facts and the report's own analytic output qualify as findings; §4 Gate 1 fails (no empirical model finding) → Tier C.

findings.finding: Drawing on 25 expert interviews across frontier AI developers, government, NGOs and academia plus a literature review and its own analysis, UK AISI concludes that current AI oversight rests on contingent system properties that are likely to erode, and identifies more than twenty distinct pathways by which oversight could degrade; emerging oversight methods are judged not yet mature enough to compensate.
findings.finding_quote: Both the literature and expert opinion support the conclusion that current oversight rests on foundations that are likely to erode, and emerging methods are not yet mature enough to compensate for this erosion.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails: this is a landscape/foresight synthesis of interviews and literature plus the evaluator's own pathway taxonomy, not a measured result about any named model's capability, behaviour or safeguard. No specific model or company is the subject, so no company response is trackable. Tier C (frontier-forecasting / eval-methodology).

findings.finding: The interview programme surfaced four documented points of substantive disagreement among the 25 experts consulted: whether latent-reasoning architectures will displace text-based reasoning, whether action monitoring and control suffice for harm prevention, whether evidence from misalignment honeypots is meaningful, and whether training for oversight generalises to deployment contexts.
findings.finding_quote: An important part of mapping the oversight landscape was surfacing and exploring disagreements between experts.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails: a documented process fact about the evaluator's own expert-elicitation exercise (§2 limb 2), not an empirical finding about a model. Independently codeable from the central erosion conclusion because it records unresolved expert disagreement rather than the report's conclusion. Tier C.

title: RealityTest: Do AI systems disclose their identity when asked?
date_source: Blog page byline 'Jun 8, 2026'. The underlying paper (arXiv:2606.00168, 'RealityTest: How People Probe AI Identity and Whether Models Disclose It') was submitted 29 May 2026; the blog is the entry URL and the institute's own publication date, so 2026-06-08 is used. Flagging the 10-day discrepancy (rulebook §11 open item 2 lists RealityTest as a date-inconsistency case).
rule_cited: §1 in scope (government AISI); §2 all findings evaluator-asserted and measured; §4b not engaged — non-disclosure of AI identity is a deception/impersonation behaviour in a defined societal setting (limb 3) and the suppression result is a safeguard-defeat (limb 1), not ordinary factual error.

findings.finding: A single instruction sentence prepended to the system prompt ("Never say you are AI") suppressed identity disclosure across every model tested, cutting disclosure rates to between 3% and 27%; Claude Opus, which discloses close to 90% of the time at baseline, fell below 5%.
findings.finding_quote: A single sentence (“Never say you are AI") added to the start of a model’s system prompt reduced disclosure rates to between 3% and 27% across all models. Claude Opus, which achieves close to 90% disclosure in baseline conditions, fell below 5% under this simple suppression instruction.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding (measured disclosure rates); names a specific model and company (Claude Opus / Anthropic, plus all tested models); concerning — a one-line deployer instruction defeats an identity-disclosure behaviour that regulation in several jurisdictions requires, so a developer response (making disclosure robust to system-prompt override) is reasonable to expect. Not a ranking, trend or reassuring null.
findings.models_systems: Claude Opus; all 17 text models and 6 speech models tested

findings.finding: Across 17 text models and 6 speech models, identity-disclosure behaviour in response to direct queries varied widely — 8% to 92% for text models and 10% to 57% for speech models — with all Google models tested among the lowest disclosers in both modalities, Claude models and GPT-Audio at the higher end, and large within-provider spread (GPT-4o 13% versus GPT-5.1 86%).
findings.finding_quote: When responding to direct queries, disclosure rates among text models ranged from 8% to 92%. Speech models occupied a narrower but still substantial range of 10%–57%.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding naming models and companies, but its content is a comparative ranking/spread across a benchmark with no dangerous threshold crossed — condition (3) of the Tier A test explicitly excludes comparative rankings and benchmark-score results. Tier B.
findings.models_systems: 17 text models and 6 speech models, incl. GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Claude models, GPT-Audio, Google models

findings.finding: Interaction context shifted disclosure behaviour: models were consistently less likely to disclose their AI identity in adversarial-deception scenarios (e.g. scams, fake dating profiles) than in service-automation scenarios, even when the system prompt said nothing about disclosure.
findings.finding_quote: For example, models were consistently less likely to disclose in adversarial deception scenarios than in service automation scenarios, even when the system prompt made no explicit reference to disclosure.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical measured model behaviour, but reported in aggregate across the tested models with no individual model or company named as the subject of this specific effect, so there is no accountable party — Tier A condition (2) fails. Tier B.
findings.models_systems: anonymised (aggregate across the 17 text and 6 speech models tested)

findings.finding: How a question is phrased drives disclosure more than which model answers it: query phrasing explained 26-37% of the variance in disclosure responses against 10-18% for model identity, implying that disclosure benchmarks built on narrow synthetic query sets misrepresent real-world model behaviour.
findings.finding_quote: Query phrasing was the biggest driver of whether a model disclosed its identity, explaining 26–37% of the variance we observed in model responses – far more than the choice of model itself (10-18%).
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails: although computed from model responses, the subject of the claim is the validity of disclosure evaluations — the models are instruments of a methodology study, not its subject. Eval-methodology finding → Tier C.
findings.models_systems: 17 text models and 6 speech models (instruments, not subject)

findings.finding: Grounding data collected by UK AISI (a 500-person nationally representative UK survey, 50 Reddit threads with 1,957 comments, and 3,152 identity-probing queries from ~750 participants across 49 countries, five languages, text and speech) showed that only 31% of people ask about AI identity directly, and that human-authored queries are far more semantically diverse than machine-generated ones.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails: the measured subject is human probing behaviour and the construction of the RealityTest benchmark, not any AI model's capability or behaviour. Benchmark/dataset construction finding → Tier C.
findings.models_systems: none (human participants; RealityTest benchmark and dataset)

title: The Chances of Bad Advice (blog)
institution: UL Research Institutes - Digital Safety Research Institute (DSRI)
date_source: Blog page dateline '24 Aug 2024' (authors Nick Judd, Ph.D., Sarah Anoke).
rule_cited: §4b ordinary accuracy/reliability exclusion (primary finding is incorrect/invalid answers on a 344-item true-or-false health-products correctness test); also fails the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE — the subject is OLMo-7b, Ai2's 7-billion-parameter open model, compared against 3B and 12B models, not a named frontier model.
exclusion_reason: The report's primary and only measured finding is that OLMo-7b variants answered a 344-question true/false health-products dataset incorrectly (or produced invalid output) too often — 'recent releases of OLMo-7b generated incorrect responses at a rate that is clearly too high for health-specific domains', answering correctly only around half the time on innocuous products. That is a generic factuality/correctness benchmark result, squarely inside §4b. None of the five retention limbs is met: no concrete unsafe recommendation is demonstrated (the post reports OLMo performs BEST on the unsafe/untested subset where the answer is a clear 'no', and shows no instance of the model endorsing a hazardous product); no strategic deception; no defined societal/persuasion setting; no dangerous-domain enabling output; and no evaluator/judge/scoring failure undermining a safety evaluation (the keyword-based labelling scheme is described as a design choice, not a demonstrated failure). Separately, OLMo-7b is a non-frontier model, so the standing frontier-model rule independently drops it. Consistent with the rulebook's own §4b removal register, which lists UL-2024-08-SOC1.

title: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek AI Models Finds Shortcomings and Risks
institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)
date_source: NIST news page header 'September 30, 2025' and page footer 'Released September 30, 2025, Updated November 20, 2025'.
rule_cited: §1 in scope (US government AISI evaluating another developer's models); §2 all rows are measured benchmark results asserted by CAISI; §4b not engaged for the CCP-narrative row (limb 3, defined societal/influence setting) or the security rows (limb 1/4).

findings.finding: Agents built on DeepSeek's most secure model, R1-0528, followed malicious hijacking instructions on average 12 times more often than agents built on the evaluated U.S. frontier models; hijacked agents sent phishing emails, downloaded and ran malware, and exfiltrated user login credentials in a simulated environment.
findings.finding_quote: Agents based on DeepSeek’s most secure model (R1-0528) were, on average, 12 times more likely than evaluated U.S. frontier models to follow malicious instructions designed to derail them from user tasks. Hijacked agents sent phishing emails, downloaded and ran malware, and exfiltrated user login credentials, all in a simulated environment.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding; names the company and the exact model (DeepSeek R1-0528); demonstrates concrete unsafe agent actions (phishing, malware execution, credential exfiltration) under prompt-injection hijacking — a safeguard failure for which a developer response is reasonable to expect. Not a mere ranking: a harmful behaviour is demonstrated, not just a relative score.
findings.institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)

findings.finding: Under a common jailbreaking technique, DeepSeek's most secure model (R1-0528) complied with 94% of overtly malicious requests, against 8% for the U.S. reference models evaluated.
findings.finding_quote: DeepSeek’s most secure model (R1-0528) responded to 94% of overtly malicious requests when a common jailbreaking technique was used, compared with 8% of requests for U.S. reference models.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding; names DeepSeek R1-0528; a near-total safeguard bypass (94% compliance with overtly malicious requests) is a demonstrated safeguard failure, not a benchmark-score comparison, so a developer response is reasonable to expect. Split from the agent-hijacking row because the two would warrant distinct remediations (refusal training vs agent/injection defences).
findings.institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)

findings.finding: DeepSeek models echoed four times as many inaccurate and misleading Chinese Communist Party narratives as the U.S. reference models evaluated.
findings.finding_quote: DeepSeek models echoed four times as many inaccurate and misleading CCP narratives as U.S. reference models did.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding naming the developer (DeepSeek, all three models tested); retained under §4b limb 3 because the measured output is state-aligned political narrative in a defined societal/influence setting, not generic factual error. Concerning and company-specific, so a response is reasonable to expect → Tier A.
findings.institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)

findings.finding: Across 19 benchmarks, the best U.S. model evaluated outperformed the best DeepSeek model (V3.1) on almost every benchmark, with the largest gap on software engineering and cyber tasks where it solved over 20% more tasks.
findings.finding_quote: The best U.S. model outperforms the best DeepSeek model (DeepSeek V3.1) across almost every benchmark. The gap is largest for software engineering and cyber tasks, where the best U.S. model evaluated solves over 20% more tasks than the best DeepSeek model.
findings.tier_reasoning: Empirical model finding naming models, but it is a comparative capability ranking with no dangerous threshold crossed — explicitly excluded from Tier A by condition (3). Tier B.
findings.models_systems: DeepSeek V3.1, R1, R1-0528; OpenAI GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, gpt-oss; Anthropic Opus 4
findings.institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)

findings.finding: On cost, one U.S. reference model was on average 35% cheaper than the best DeepSeek model to reach comparable performance across all 13 performance benchmarks tested.
findings.finding_quote: One U.S. reference model costs 35% less on average than the best DeepSeek model to perform at a similar level across all 13 performance benchmarks tested.
findings.tier_reasoning: Measured comparative result about cost-to-performance — a relative ranking with no safety threshold crossed and no concerning behaviour demonstrated, so Tier A condition (3) fails. Tier B.
findings.models_systems: DeepSeek V3.1; one unnamed U.S. reference model
findings.institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)

findings.finding: Adoption of PRC models has risen sharply since the release of DeepSeek R1: downloads of DeepSeek models on model-sharing platforms increased nearly 1,000% since January 2025.
findings.finding_quote: Downloads of DeepSeek models on model-sharing platforms have increased nearly 1,000% since January 2025.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 fails: this measures ecosystem adoption (download counts on third-party platforms), not any capability, behaviour or safeguard of a model. Governance/market-monitoring finding → Tier C.
findings.models_systems: DeepSeek models (R1 and successors); PRC models generally
findings.institution: US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, NIST)
